subject: ENG
label: Grade 12 Humanities
task: Meet the outcome of every unit in Grade 12 Humanities English, and keep one piece of evidence for each.

modules.title: Prose and poetry from world writers
modules.outcome: compare two authors' treatment of one theme
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Prose and poetry from world writers', taught in a way that is with exam-style questions and written reasoning. The target is clear: compare two authors' treatment of one theme. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Listen first: your teacher or a recording says the new words or sentences from 'Prose and poetry from world writers' twice. You repeat them aloud.
Notice the pattern: find where the new sound, word form or sentence rule appears in a short text and mark it.
Use it: compare two authors' treatment of one theme, first with help, then alone.
Check and fix: read your work aloud once more; fix one thing you hear is wrong.
modules.example: Solved: Simile: 'The moon is like a silver coin.' Metaphor: 'The classroom was a zoo.' Imagery: 'the dew-wet grass' appeals to sight and touch. Say what feeling each creates. Method: Model run for 'Prose and poetry from world writers'. Teacher text (3 lines about a daily activity). Step 1, read it aloud together. Step 2, mark every word or sentence that uses the new pattern. Step 3, a learner writes or says two new lines of their own that use the same pattern. Step 4, the learner reads them aloud and corrects one slip. What a good answer looks like: the pattern is used correctly in both lines, the lines make sense, and the learner can say which part is the pattern.
modules.activity: About 40 to 50 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a timed paper and an error log.
modules.standard: Compare two authors' treatment of one theme: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown.
steps: Step 1, State the shared theme as a sentence. Extract A (prose): 'Amira packed only what the case would hold. At the gate she turned once, and the olive tree seemed to lean toward her.' Extract B (poem): 'I carry the street in my pocket, / its noise folded small.' Theme: leaving home means carrying loss and belonging together.

Step 2, Gather evidence from A. 'Only what the case would hold' shows that leaving forces hard choices. The olive tree 'seemed to lean toward her': personification shows the place itself reluctant to let her go. Write the quotation, then name the technique, then say the effect.

Step 3, Gather evidence from B. 'I carry the street in my pocket' is a metaphor: a whole home shrinks to something portable. 'Its noise folded small' suggests memory has to be made quiet and small to survive in a new place. The speaker is already abroad, so the mood is lonely.

Step 4, Build a comparison grid. Similarity: both treat home as something that cannot be fully packed. Difference: A shows the moment of departure, with the place almost alive, whereas B shows life after arrival, with the place reduced to memory. Use linking words: similarly, whereas, however, in contrast.

Step 5, Write one comparative paragraph. 'Both writers present leaving home as loss. In A, the tree that 'seemed to lean' suggests the homeland resists parting; similarly, in B the street 'folded small' shows memory shrinking. However, A focuses on the departure itself, whereas B reflects on its aftermath.' Quote exactly and compare in each sentence.

Step 6, Your turn: compare 'only what the case would hold' (A) with 'folded small' (B) in two sentences. Model answer: Both phrases show that a whole life must be reduced to fit what can be carried. A's limit is physical, a case, whereas B's is emotional, memory folded small, so A stresses choice and B stresses endurance.

modules.title: Grammar and editing
modules.outcome: edit and transform text with precision
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Grammar and editing', taught in a way that is with exam-style questions and written reasoning. The target is clear: edit and transform text with precision. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Listen first: your teacher or a recording says the new words or sentences from 'Grammar and editing' twice. You repeat them aloud.
Notice the pattern: find where the new sound, word form or sentence rule appears in a short text and mark it.
Use it: edit and transform text with precision, first with help, then alone.
Check and fix: read your work aloud once more; fix one thing you hear is wrong.
modules.example: Solved: Passive: 'The cat chased the mouse' becomes 'The mouse was chased by the cat.' Reported: 'I will come,' she said becomes She said that she would come. Modals: 'should' for advice, 'must' for rules. Agreement: 'The list of items is long.' Edit: 'He go to school' becomes 'He goes to school.' Method: Model run for 'Grammar and editing'. Teacher text (3 lines about a daily activity). Step 1, read it aloud together. Step 2, mark every word or sentence that uses the new pattern. Step 3, a learner writes or says two new lines of their own that use the same pattern. Step 4, the learner reads them aloud and corrects one slip. What a good answer looks like: the pattern is used correctly in both lines, the lines make sense, and the learner can say which part is the pattern.
modules.activity: About 40 to 50 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a timed paper and an error log.
modules.standard: Edit and transform text with precision: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown.
steps: Step 1, Edit for dangling modifiers. 'Walking through the museum, the exhibits impressed us.' The opening phrase must describe the subject, but exhibits cannot walk. Fix: 'Walking through the museum, we were impressed by the exhibits.' Ask who is doing the action in the opening phrase, then make that person the subject.

Step 2, Edit punctuation with 'however'. 'The empire grew quickly, however it fell slowly.' A comma cannot join two sentences. Correct: 'The empire grew quickly; however, it fell slowly.' The semicolon links the two ideas, and 'however' takes a comma after it. Alternatively use a full stop before 'However'.

Step 3, Keep tenses consistent. 'In 1948 the delegates signed the charter and celebrations are held across the city.' Both events are in the past, so write 'were held'. Underline every verb in the paragraph, mark its time, and change any that shift without a reason such as a general truth.

Step 4, Repair parallel structure. 'The historian likes reading, to write and researching archives.' The three items must share one form: 'The historian likes reading, writing and researching archives.' Lists, comparisons and 'not only ... but also' pairs all need the same grammatical pattern on each side.

Step 5, Transform a question into reported speech. Direct: She asked, 'Where did the army march?' Reported: She asked where the army had marched. Notice there is no question mark, the word order is statement order, and the past tense shifts back to the past perfect.

Step 6, Your turn: edit 'The council met in March, however nobody agreed' and report 'He asked, 'Why is the bridge closed?'' Answer: 'The council met in March; however, nobody agreed.' Reported: He asked why the bridge was closed.

modules.title: Writing: reports, letters and articles
modules.outcome: write formal, persuasive and analytical text
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Writing: reports, letters and articles', taught in a way that is with exam-style questions and written reasoning. The target is clear: write formal, persuasive and analytical text. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Listen first: your teacher or a recording says the new words or sentences from 'Writing: reports, letters and articles' twice. You repeat them aloud.
Notice the pattern: find where the new sound, word form or sentence rule appears in a short text and mark it.
Use it: write formal, persuasive and analytical text, first with help, then alone.
Check and fix: read your work aloud once more; fix one thing you hear is wrong.
modules.example: Solved: Formal letter: 12 November 2026; The Principal; Subject: request for a library card; 'Respected Sir, I am a student of Class 8...'; Yours faithfully, Aman. Informal: Dear Ria, ... Your friend, Aman. Report: title, date, place, what happened, result, writer's name. Method: Model run for 'Writing: reports, letters and articles'. Teacher text (3 lines about a daily activity). Step 1, read it aloud together. Step 2, mark every word or sentence that uses the new pattern. Step 3, a learner writes or says two new lines of their own that use the same pattern. Step 4, the learner reads them aloud and corrects one slip. What a good answer looks like: the pattern is used correctly in both lines, the lines make sense, and the learner can say which part is the pattern.
modules.activity: About 40 to 50 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a timed paper and an error log.
modules.standard: Write formal, persuasive and analytical text: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown.
steps: Step 1, Plan a letter to the editor. Issue: a plan to close the town library on weekends. Facts: weekly visits are 1,200, and 450 of them happen on Saturday and Sunday, which is 37.5 per cent. Layout: address, date, 'Dear Editor', a subject line, three paragraphs, 'Yours faithfully'.

Step 2, Write the opening and argument. 'I am writing to oppose the plan to close the library at weekends. Of the 1,200 visits made each week, 450, or 37.5 per cent, take place on Saturday and Sunday, when working families can come.' Open with your position, then support it with a figure.

Step 3, Add counter-argument and appeal. 'Some may argue that weekday opening is enough. However, students in school and adults at work cannot use it then.' Answering the opposing view makes the writing persuasive. End: 'I urge the council to keep weekend hours.'

Step 4, Write an analytical report. Survey of 80 students: 56 use the library at least weekly. 56 out of 80 is 70 per cent. Headings: Introduction, Findings, Conclusion, Recommendations. Finding: 'Seventy per cent of students use the library weekly.' Recommendation: extend evening hours.

Step 5, Draft a feature article. Headline: 'Voices Worth Keeping'. Hook: 'Every elder in our village is a living archive.' Develop with a short anecdote, one fact and a quotation, and close with a call to action. Persuasive articles use an engaging headline, vivid detail and a firm final sentence.

Step 6, Your turn: calculate and write one sentence for a report if 18 of 45 residents prefer evening opening. Answer: 18 out of 45 is 40 per cent. 'Forty per cent of the residents surveyed prefer the library to open in the evening, which suggests that evening hours should be considered.'

modules.title: Reading: unseen passages
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Reading: unseen passages', taught in a way that is with exam-style questions and written reasoning. The target is clear: read critically in timed conditions. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Listen first: your teacher or a recording says the new words or sentences from 'Reading: unseen passages' twice. You repeat them aloud.
Notice the pattern: find where the new sound, word form or sentence rule appears in a short text and mark it.
Use it: read critically in timed conditions, first with help, then alone.
Check and fix: read your work aloud once more; fix one thing you hear is wrong.
modules.example: Solved: Passage: 'The old banyan tree gave shade to the whole village.' Q: what does 'shade' suggest? Protection from the sun. Inference: the tree matters to the villagers. Answer with a quote as evidence. Method: Model run for 'Reading: unseen passages'. Teacher text (3 lines about a daily activity). Step 1, read it aloud together. Step 2, mark every word or sentence that uses the new pattern. Step 3, a learner writes or says two new lines of their own that use the same pattern. Step 4, the learner reads them aloud and corrects one slip. What a good answer looks like: the pattern is used correctly in both lines, the lines make sense, and the learner can say which part is the pattern.
modules.activity: About 40 to 50 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a timed paper and an error log.
modules.standard: Read critically in timed conditions: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown.
steps: Step 1, Plan the timing. For a 45-minute unseen section, spend 5 minutes skimming, 30 answering and 10 checking. Passage: 'A village project recorded 45 interviews with older residents. Eighteen of the speakers were over 80. The average interview lasted 32 minutes. Some historians doubt memories, yet the project argues that stories reveal what documents omit.'

Step 2, Skim and annotate. Circle the numbers (45, 18, 32), underline 'doubt' and 'yet', and note the main idea: personal memories add something that official records do not, even if they are imperfect. This takes about two minutes and shows the shape of the argument.

Step 3, Answer the number questions. 18 of 45 speakers over 80 is 40 per cent. Total recorded time is 45 x 32 = 1,440 minutes, which is 24 hours. Show the working and add units. Quote 'eighteen' and 'average interview lasted 32 minutes' as evidence.

Step 4, Read critically. 'Some historians doubt memories, yet the project argues...' The word 'yet' signals a counter-claim, and 'argues' presents it as a view, not a fact. A critical reader asks whether the project is neutral. The evidence is one village, so the claim may not apply everywhere.

Step 5, Handle vocabulary and summary. 'Omit' means 'leave out', which the contrast with 'reveal' makes clear. A 35-word summary: 'A village project recorded 45 interviews, 40 per cent with people over 80, arguing that memories show what documents leave out, despite doubts from some historians.' Use your own words.

Step 6, Your turn: state one opposing view in the passage and one limit of the evidence. Answer: Some historians doubt memories (the opposing view). The limit is that the evidence comes from one village, so it may not represent everywhere. Quote 'some historians doubt memories'.

Teacher text (3 lines about a daily activity). Step 1, read it aloud together. Step 2, mark every word or sentence that uses the new pattern. modules.activity: About 40 to 50 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a timed paper and an error log.
modules.standard: Deliver an argued presentation: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown.
steps: Step 1, Frame the motion. "Societies should preserve minority languages." Thesis: "Minority languages carry knowledge and identity that cannot be translated fully." Reason: a precise thesis lets you choose relevant evidence.
Step 2, Write an engaging opening. "When the last speaker of a language dies, a library of stories, remedies and humour disappears. We lose more than words." Reason: a vivid image shows the stakes.

Step 3, Build argument one with PEEL. Point: languages store knowledge. Evidence: many communities have terms for local plants and seasons. Explain: losing the language risks losing practical knowledge. Link: preservation is a duty.

Step 4, Address a counter-argument. "Critics say one common language is more efficient. Efficiency matters, but multilingual societies show that people can learn a common language and keep their own." Reason: concede, then show both can coexist.

Step 5, Fix an error. Weak: "Everyone knows languages are important." Better: "Linguists estimate that a language disappears every few weeks, so the pace of loss is serious." Use specific evidence, not appeal to common belief.

Step 6, Close with force. "To preserve a language is to preserve a way of seeing. Let us fund schools, archives and broadcasts so that no voice falls silent." Reason: a call to action leaves a clear final impression.

Step 7, Your turn. Write a thesis and one counter-argument for "Museums should return cultural objects to their places of origin". Model answer: "Thesis: Returning objects restores dignity and context." "Counter: Some fear loss of access; digital copies and loans can keep both."
